title: Acute epiglottitis – Definition
content: Acute epiglottitis is a severe inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic tissues, posing a significant risk of swift airway blockage. While historically prevalent in children aged 2-7, its incidence has shifted towards adults, largely due to the Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccine.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Epidemiology
content: The incidence of acute epiglottitis is approximately 2 per 100,000 person-years. Although its demographic has shifted, it is still most frequently observed in infants.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Aetiology
content: Historically, Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) was the primary bacterial cause of acute epiglottitis. Current bacterial pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Group A streptococci, and Staphylococcus aureus. Viral, fungal, and non-infectious factors like thermal injury can also contribute.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Clinical features
content: Patients with acute epiglottitis often present with a severe sore throat and painful swallowing (odynophagia), leading to drooling. A muffled 'hot potato' voice is characteristic, along with high-pitched inspiratory stridor and respiratory distress with tachypnea.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Clinical features
content: A high-grade fever is a common clinical feature of acute epiglottitis. Patients may adopt a tripod or sniffing position, leaning forward with a chin thrust and open mouth, to facilitate breathing.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Clinical features
content: Crucially, direct examination of the throat in suspected acute epiglottitis is contraindicated due to the significant risk of precipitating acute airway obstruction, which can be life-threatening.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Investigations
content: A lateral neck radiograph is a key investigation for acute epiglottitis, often revealing the characteristic 'thumb sign,' indicative of a swollen epiglottis.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Investigations
content: Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy, performed only by experienced personnel, can directly visualize the inflamed epiglottis and supraglottic structures, aiding in diagnosis and assessing airway compromise.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Investigations
content: Blood cultures and throat swabs are essential investigations to identify the causative pathogen in acute epiglottitis, guiding targeted antibiotic therapy.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Management
content: Airway management is paramount in acute epiglottitis and typically occurs in an Intensive Care Unit (ICU) setting. Endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy may be required to secure the airway and prevent obstruction.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Management
content: Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as third-generation cephalosporins, are initiated promptly to cover common bacterial pathogens while awaiting culture results.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Management
content: Supportive care for acute epiglottitis includes intravenous fluids to maintain hydration, analgesics for pain relief, and antipyretics to manage fever. The use of corticosteroids remains controversial.

title: Acute epiglottitis – Prevention
content: Prevention of acute epiglottitis is primarily achieved through Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccination, which has significantly reduced the incidence of the disease, especially in children.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Definition
content: Genital herpes is a prevalent viral sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by either Herpes Simplex Virus type 1 (HSV-1) or type 2 (HSV-2).

title: Herpes simplex virus – Definition
content: Herpes simplex virus establishes a lifelong infection, remaining dormant (latent) within the sensory neurons of the affected individual.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Definition
content: Transmission of genital herpes is possible even when an infected individual exhibits no visible symptoms, a phenomenon known as asymptomatic shedding.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Epidemiology
content: The incidence of genital herpes is approximately 300 cases per 100,000 person-years, indicating its common occurrence.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Epidemiology
content: The peak incidence of genital herpes is observed in individuals between 20 and 30 years of age.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Genital herpes is predominantly caused by HSV-2, but HSV-1 is increasingly responsible for genital infections, often due to orogenital contact.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: A significant risk factor for acquiring genital herpes is having multiple sexual partners.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: The presence of other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) increases the risk of contracting genital herpes.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Female sex is identified as a risk factor for genital herpes infection.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Immunosuppression is a recognized risk factor that can increase susceptibility to genital herpes.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
content: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) initiates infection by adhering to heparan sulphate molecules present on the surface of host cells.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
content: Following adhesion, HSV enters the host cell and proceeds to replicate its genetic material within the cell's nucleus.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
content: After replication, the virus spreads to the sensory nerve endings, marking a critical step in its dissemination.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
content: Retrograde transport of HSV to the dorsal root ganglia leads to the establishment of a latent infection.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
content: Reactivation of latent HSV can be triggered by various factors, including UV light exposure, psychological stress, and immunosuppression.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
content: Upon reactivation, HSV undergoes anterograde transport, moving back along the nerve to the epidermis, where lesions typically appear.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
content: Primary genital herpes often presents with grouped, painful blisters that typically rupture after 2-3 days.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
content: After blistering, crusted erosions or ulcers form on the external genitalia, characteristic of primary genital herpes.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
content: Lesions associated with primary genital herpes can extend to the thigh, buttocks, cervix, and rectum.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
content: Dysuria, or painful urination, is a common symptom in women experiencing primary genital herpes.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
content: Urinary retention can occur in severe cases of primary genital herpes, particularly in women.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
content: Inguinal lymphadenopathy, swelling of lymph nodes in the groin, is observed in approximately 30% of primary genital herpes cases.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
content: Around 50% of individuals with primary genital herpes experience systemic illness, including headache, fever, myalgia, and general malaise.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
content: The symptoms of primary genital herpes can persist for up to 20 days, making it a prolonged initial episode.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (recurrent)
content: Recurrent genital herpes episodes are often preceded by a prodrome of tingling or burning sensations up to 48 hours before lesion appearance.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (recurrent)
content: Lesions during recurrent episodes of genital herpes are typically less severe and tend to appear in the same anatomical area as previous outbreaks.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (recurrent)
content: Recurrent genital herpes lesions generally heal within 10 days, a shorter duration compared to primary infections.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Investigations
content: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) or Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) is the first-line investigation for genital herpes, as per BASHH 2014 guidelines.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Investigations
content: Viral culture may be utilized for diagnosing genital herpes if PCR/NAAT testing is not readily available.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Investigations
content: Serology for HSV type-specific IgG antibodies can be performed to determine past exposure and differentiate between HSV-1 and HSV-2.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Management
content: Antiviral therapy, including medications like aciclovir, valaciclovir, and famciclovir, is used to manage genital herpes.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Management
content: Antiviral therapy for genital herpes effectively reduces the severity and duration of outbreaks but does not provide a cure for the infection.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Management
content: For individuals experiencing frequent recurrences of genital herpes, suppressive antiviral therapy may be prescribed to reduce outbreak frequency.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Definition
content: Bacterial vaginosis is characterized by an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria, primarily Gardnerella vaginalis, coupled with a reduction in beneficial lactic acid-producing lactobacilli, leading to an elevated vaginal pH.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Association with sexual activity
content: Although not classified as a sexually transmitted infection (STI), bacterial vaginosis is observed almost exclusively in women who are sexually active.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Incidence
content: The incidence of bacterial vaginosis is approximately 5,000 cases per 100,000 person-years, indicating its prevalence within the population.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Peak age
content: Bacterial vaginosis most commonly affects women between 20 and 30 years of age, representing the peak incidence period for this condition.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Abnormal vaginal discharge
content: A key clinical feature of bacterial vaginosis is an abnormal vaginal discharge, often described as having a 'fishy' odor.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Odor characteristics
content: The characteristic 'fishy' odor associated with bacterial vaginosis typically worsens after sexual intercourse, during menstruation, or following washing with soap.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Asymptomatic presentation
content: Approximately 50% of individuals with bacterial vaginosis may not experience any noticeable symptoms, making it an often asymptomatic condition.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Discharge appearance
content: The vaginal discharge in bacterial vaginosis is typically thin, homogeneous, and white-grey, often coating the vaginal walls.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Absence of itching
content: Unlike candidiasis, bacterial vaginosis typically does not present with vulval or vaginal itching.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Absence of other symptoms
content: Patients with bacterial vaginosis usually do not experience dysuria, dyspareunia, or abdominal pain.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Amsel's criteria
content: Diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis is typically made using Amsel's criteria, requiring at least three out of four specific clinical findings.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Amsel's criteria components
content: Amsel's criteria include thin white homogeneous discharge, presence of clue cells on microscopy, vaginal pH >4.5, and a positive whiff test.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Asymptomatic management
content: Treatment for asymptomatic bacterial vaginosis is generally not required, except in specific situations such as prior to termination of pregnancy.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Symptomatic management
content: Symptomatic bacterial vaginosis is typically managed with oral metronidazole for 5-7 days, achieving a 70-80% cure rate, though relapse within 3 months is common.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Single dose metronidazole
content: A single 2g dose of metronidazole can be considered for symptomatic bacterial vaginosis if there are concerns regarding patient adherence to a longer course.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Alternative treatments
content: Alternative treatment options for bacterial vaginosis include topical metronidazole or topical clindamycin.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Management in pregnancy
content: In pregnant women, oral metronidazole is recommended throughout pregnancy, including the first trimester, according to recent guidelines.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Increased STI susceptibility
content: A complication of bacterial vaginosis is an increased susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections, including HIV.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Increased PID risk
content: Bacterial vaginosis increases the risk of developing pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), a serious infection of the female reproductive organs.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Pregnancy complications
content: In pregnancy, bacterial vaginosis is associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes such as preterm birth, premature rupture of membranes, and postpartum endometritis.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Definition
content: Campylobacter jejuni is a gram-negative, spiral-shaped bacterium. It is recognized as one of the most frequent bacterial causes of gastroenteritis globally.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Campylobacter jejuni is the causative agent, characterized as a gram-negative, curved or spiral-shaped, non-sporulating bacterium.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Transmission of Campylobacter infection primarily occurs through consumption of undercooked poultry, unpasteurised milk, or contaminated water sources.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Clinical features
content: The incubation period for Campylobacter infection typically ranges from 1 to 3 days, preceding the onset of symptoms.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Clinical features
content: Patients may experience a prodrome including fever, headache, and myalgia before the main gastrointestinal symptoms manifest.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Clinical features
content: Key symptoms include diarrhoea, which can be bloody, accompanied by abdominal cramping, nausea, and vomiting.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Clinical features
content: The infection is typically self-limiting, with symptoms usually resolving within 5 to 7 days without specific intervention.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Investigations
content: Stool culture remains the gold standard for diagnosing Campylobacter infection, though PCR testing is increasingly utilized for detection.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Management
content: Management of Campylobacter infection primarily involves fluid replacement, as antibiotics are not routinely advised due to the self-limiting nature.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Management
content: For severe cases or immunocompromised patients, azithromycin is the first-line antibiotic, with ciprofloxacin as an alternative despite increasing resistance.

title: Notifiable diseases – Management
content: Campylobacter infection is classified as a notifiable disease, requiring reporting to public health authorities for surveillance and control.

title: Infectious diarrhoea – Complications
content: Potential complications of Campylobacter infection include reactive arthritis, Guillain-Barré syndrome (due to molecular mimicry), and rarely, haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

title: Cellulitis – Definition
content: Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection affecting the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue.

title: Erysipelas – Definition
content: Erysipelas is a more superficial form of bacterial infection, specifically affecting the dermis and superficial subcutaneous tissue.

title: Cellulitis – Epidemiology
content: Cellulitis is a common condition. It typically presents unilaterally; bilateral cellulitis is rare and suggests an alternative diagnosis.

title: Cellulitis – Most Common Pathogen
content: The most common pathogen causing cellulitis is Streptococcus pyogenes, also known as Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus.

title: Cellulitis – Second Most Common Pathogen
content: Staphylococcus aureus, including Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), is the second most common pathogen in cellulitis.

title: Cellulitis – Risk Factors (Skin/Medical)
content: Risk factors for cellulitis include tinea pedis, eczema/psoriasis, diabetes, intravenous drug use (IVDU), alcoholism, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.

title: Cellulitis – Clinical Features (Local)
content: Clinical features of cellulitis include erythema with reasonably well-defined margins, swelling, warmth, and tenderness, commonly on the shins.

title: Cellulitis – Clinical Features (Severe)
content: In severe cellulitis, blisters or bullae may be present. Systemic upset can manifest as fever, malaise, and nausea.

title: Cellulitis – Investigations (Blood Tests)
content: Investigations for cellulitis include a Full Blood Count (FBC) which may show leucocytosis, and Urea & Electrolytes (U&E) where AKI indicates systemic response.

title: Cellulitis – Investigations (Inflammatory Markers)
content: C-reactive protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) are inflammatory markers used in the investigation of cellulitis.

title: Cellulitis – Investigations (Cultures)
content: A wound swab is only indicated if the wound is open or weeping. Blood cultures should be taken if there is a significant systemic response.

title: Cellulitis – Eron Classification Class I
content: Eron Class I cellulitis presents with no systemic toxicity and no uncontrolled comorbidities.

title: Cellulitis – Eron Classification Class II
content: Eron Class II cellulitis indicates the patient is systemically unwell OR has comorbidities that are not well-controlled.

title: Cellulitis – Eron Classification Class III
content: Eron Class III cellulitis involves significant systemic upset, such as confusion, tachycardia, or hypotension, or is limb-threatening.

title: Cellulitis – Eron Classification Class IV
content: Eron Class IV cellulitis signifies sepsis or a severe, life-threatening condition like necrotising fasciitis.

title: Cellulitis – Management (Class I Oral)
content: For Eron Class I cellulitis, oral flucloxacillin is the first-line treatment. Alternatives for penicillin allergy include clarithromycin, erythromycin, or doxycycline.

title: Cellulitis – Management (Class III-IV IV)
content: Patients with Eron Class III-IV cellulitis require admission and intravenous antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav, clindamycin, cefuroxime, or ceftriaxone.

title: Cellulitis – Management (Supportive Care)
content: Supportive management for cellulitis includes marking the erythema margins to monitor spread and elevating the affected leg.

title: Cellulitis – Admission Criteria (Severity)
content: Admission criteria for cellulitis include Eron Class III/IV, severe or rapidly deteriorating condition, or very young (<1 year) or frail patients.

title: Cellulitis – Admission Criteria (Specific Cases)
content: Specific cases requiring admission for cellulitis include immunocompromised patients, those with significant lymphoedema, or facial/periorbital cellulitis.

title: Hepatitis A – Definition
content: Hepatitis A is a viral hepatitis caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV), an RNA picornavirus. It is primarily transmitted via the faecal-oral route and notably does not lead to chronic infection.

title: Hepatitis A – Epidemiology (Incidence)
content: The incidence of Hepatitis A is approximately 1.2 per 100,000 person-years. This viral infection shows a peak incidence in individuals aged between 30 and 40 years.

title: Hepatitis A – Aetiology (Virus)
content: Hepatitis A is caused by the Hepatitis A Virus (HAV), which is classified as an RNA picornavirus.

title: Hepatitis A – Aetiology (Transmission)
content: Transmission of Hepatitis A occurs via the faecal-oral route, often through contaminated food or water, shellfish, travel to endemic areas, men who have sex with men (MSM), and intravenous drug users (IVDU).

title: Hepatitis A – Clinical Features (Incubation)
content: The incubation period for Hepatitis A typically ranges from 2 to 6 weeks.

title: Hepatitis A – Clinical Features (Prodrome)
content: The prodromal symptoms of Hepatitis A include fever, general malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

title: Hepatitis A – Clinical Features (Jaundice)
content: Jaundice in Hepatitis A presents with dark urine, pale stools, and pruritus. Hepatomegaly is also a common finding.

title: Hepatitis A – Clinical Features (Course)
content: Hepatitis A is typically a self-limiting infection, with most individuals recovering without specific treatment.

title: Hepatitis A – Investigations (Serology)
content: Serological testing for Hepatitis A includes anti-HAV IgM, indicating acute infection, and anti-HAV IgG, which signifies past infection or immunity.

title: Hepatitis A – Investigations (Liver Function Tests)
content: Investigations for Hepatitis A typically reveal elevated Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) and Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST), along with raised bilirubin levels.

title: Hepatitis A – Management (Supportive Care)
content: Management of Hepatitis A is primarily supportive, focusing on symptom relief. Patients should avoid alcohol for 6 months and hepatotoxic drugs.

title: Hepatitis A – Management (Public Health & Follow-up)
content: Hepatitis A is a notifiable disease, requiring public health notification. Follow-up with Liver Function Tests (LFTs) is necessary until they normalize.

title: Hepatitis A – Management (Post-exposure Prophylaxis)
content: Post-exposure prophylaxis for Hepatitis A involves either the HAV vaccine (preferred) or Human Normal Immunoglobulin (HNIG) for those unable to receive the vaccine.

title: Hepatitis A – Complications (Common)
content: The majority of individuals with Hepatitis A recover fully within 6 months. However, a relapsing course can occur in 15% of cases.

title: Hepatitis A – Complications (Severe)
content: Severe complications of Hepatitis A include fulminant liver failure (0.4%). Rare complications include acalculous cholecystitis, pancreatitis, aplastic anaemia, post-viral encephalitis, and reactive arthritis.

title: Hepatitis A – Prognosis
content: The overall mortality rate for Hepatitis A is approximately 0.1%, increasing to 1.8% in individuals over 50 years of age. Importantly, Hepatitis A does not lead to chronic infection.

title: Hepatitis B – Definition
content: Hepatitis B is a viral liver inflammation caused by the Hepatitis B virus (HBV), an enveloped, partially double-stranded DNA virus. It can lead to both acute and chronic liver conditions.

title: Hepatitis B – Epidemiology
content: The incidence of Hepatitis B is approximately 0.8 cases per 100,000 person-years, indicating its prevalence within the population.

title: Hepatitis B – Epidemiology
content: Hepatitis B shows a peak incidence in individuals aged 30 to 40 years, suggesting a higher risk of new infections within this demographic.

title: Hepatitis B – Epidemiology
content: Globally, there are approximately 250 million carriers of Hepatitis B, highlighting its significant worldwide burden.

title: Hepatitis B – Aetiology/Transmission
content: Perinatal transmission is the most common route in endemic areas, with over 90% risk without immunisation.

title: Hepatitis B – Aetiology/Transmission
content: Sexual transmission of Hepatitis B is prevalent among men who have sex with men (MSM), sex workers, and individuals with multiple partners.

title: Hepatitis B – Aetiology/Transmission
content: Percutaneous transmission occurs through intravenous drug use (IVDU) needle sharing, tattoos, and piercings.

title: Hepatitis B – Aetiology/Transmission
content: Blood transfusion as a source of Hepatitis B is now rare due to rigorous screening protocols.

title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
content: Liver damage in Hepatitis B is primarily immune-mediated, resulting from cytotoxic T-cell lysis of infected hepatocytes.

title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
content: CD4+ T-cells activate CD8+ T-cells, which then release IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha, contributing to liver inflammation.

title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
content: The immune tolerance phase of HBV infection is characterized by high HBV DNA levels with no significant liver damage.

title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
content: The immune clearance/active phase involves HBeAg clearance and active liver damage.

title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
content: Immune control phase signifies remission with normalized liver function tests (LFTs).

title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
content: Immune escape refers to reactivation of the virus, potentially leading to renewed liver damage.

title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
content: HBsAg (surface antigen) indicates active acute or chronic Hepatitis B infection.

title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
content: Anti-HBs (protective antibody) signifies either past infection with recovery or successful vaccination.

title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
content: HBeAg indicates active viral replication and high infectivity.

title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
content: Anti-HBe suggests reduced viral replication and lower infectivity.

title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
content: Anti-HBc IgM is a marker for acute Hepatitis B infection.

title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
content: Anti-HBc IgG indicates either past or chronic Hepatitis B infection.

title: Hepatitis B – Clinical features (acute)
content: The majority of acute Hepatitis B infections are asymptomatic.

title: Hepatitis B – Clinical features (acute)
content: Symptomatic acute Hepatitis B can present with fatigue, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain.

title: Hepatitis B – Clinical features (acute)
content: Fulminant hepatitis is a rare but severe complication of acute Hepatitis B, occurring in less than 1% of cases.

title: Hepatitis B – Clinical features (chronic)
content: Chronic Hepatitis B is defined by the persistence of HBsAg positivity for more than six months.

title: Hepatitis B – Clinical features (chronic)
content: Chronic Hepatitis B increases the risk of developing serious complications such as cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

title: Hepatitis B – Management
content: Acute Hepatitis B infection is managed with supportive care.

title: Hepatitis B – Management
content: Chronic Hepatitis B is treated with antiviral medications such as tenofovir, entecavir, and pegylated interferon.

title: Hepatitis B – Management
content: Hepatitis B vaccination involves a 3-dose schedule (0, 1, and 6 months), with an accelerated schedule also available.

title: Hepatitis B – Prevention
content: Prevention includes vaccination of neonates born to HBsAg-positive mothers with HBIG and vaccine within 24 hours of birth.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Definition
content: HIV is a lentivirus, an RNA retrovirus that causes progressive immunodeficiency by targeting immune cells.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Variants
content: There are two main variants of HIV: HIV-1, which is globally prevalent, and HIV-2, primarily found in West Africa, known for lower transmission rates and slower disease progression.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Epidemiology
content: The peak incidence of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection is typically observed in individuals between 30 and 40 years of age.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Sexual Transmission
content: HIV is primarily transmitted through sexual contact, with unprotected receptive anal intercourse carrying the highest risk of transmission.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Parenteral Transmission
content: Parenteral transmission of HIV occurs through routes such as sharing needles among intravenous drug users and accidental needlestick injuries.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Vertical Transmission
content: Vertical transmission of HIV from mother to child can occur during pregnancy, childbirth, or through breastfeeding.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Blood Transfusion Risk
content: Transmission of HIV via blood transfusion is now rare in settings where blood products are routinely screened for the virus.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Genetic Resistance
content: Individuals with the CCR5-delta32 genetic mutation exhibit natural resistance to HIV infection, as it prevents the virus from entering cells.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Viral Entry
content: The HIV gp120 protein binds to CD4 receptors and either CXCR4 (on T cells) or CCR5 (on macrophages) to gain entry into host cells.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Reverse Transcription
content: HIV's reverse transcriptase enzyme converts its RNA genome into double-stranded DNA, which is then integrated into the host cell's genome.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Immunodeficiency Mechanism
content: HIV progressively destroys CD4+ T cells, leading to a compromised immune system and the development of immunodeficiency.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Seroconversion Timing
content: Seroconversion, the period when HIV antibodies become detectable, typically occurs 3 to 12 weeks following initial infection.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Seroconversion Symptoms
content: Approximately 60-80% of individuals experience symptomatic seroconversion, presenting with a glandular fever-like illness.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Glandular Fever-like Illness
content: Symptoms of acute HIV seroconversion can include sore throat, lymphadenopathy, malaise, myalgia, arthralgia, diarrhoea, maculopapular rash, and mouth ulcers.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Seroconversion Meningoencephalitis
content: In rare cases, acute HIV seroconversion may manifest with meningoencephalitis, indicating central nervous system involvement.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - CD4 200-500 Complications
content: With CD4 counts between 200-500 cells/mm³, HIV patients may develop oral thrush (Candida), shingles (VZV), hairy leukoplakia (EBV), and Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8).

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - CD4 100-200 Complications
content: When CD4 counts fall to 100-200 cells/mm³, complications such as cryptosporidiosis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, PML (JC virus), PCP (Pneumocystis jirovecii), and HIV dementia can occur.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - CD4 50-100 Complications
content: At CD4 counts of 50-100 cells/mm³, patients are susceptible to aspergillosis, oesophageal candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis, and primary CNS lymphoma (EBV).

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - CD4 <50 Complications
content: With CD4 counts below 50 cells/mm³, severe complications like CMV retinitis and Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection are common.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - HIV Antibody/Antigen Test
content: Initial diagnosis of HIV involves an antibody/antigen test, which detects both p24 antigen and HIV antibodies.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - HIV RNA Viral Load
content: HIV RNA viral load testing quantifies the amount of HIV genetic material in the blood, indicating disease activity and treatment effectiveness.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - CD4 T-cell Count
content: CD4 T-cell count measures the number of CD4+ T lymphocytes, a key indicator of immune system health and HIV disease progression.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Resistance Testing
content: Resistance testing is performed before initiating Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) to identify viral mutations that may confer resistance to specific drugs.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - HAART Initiation
content: Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) should be initiated immediately upon diagnosis of HIV, as per 2015 BHIVA guidelines.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - HAART Regimen
content: A typical HAART regimen consists of two Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) combined with either a Protease Inhibitor (PI) or a Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NNRTI).

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Entry Inhibitors
content: Entry inhibitors for HIV include maraviroc, which blocks the CCR5 co-receptor, and enfuvirtide, which targets the gp41 fusion protein.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - NRTIs
content: Common Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) used in HIV treatment include zidovudine, abacavir, tenofovir, and emtricitabine.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - NNRTIs
content: Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) commonly prescribed for HIV include nevirapine and efavirenz.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - PIs
content: Protease Inhibitors (PIs) used in HIV therapy include indinavir and ritonavir, with ritonavir also acting as a P450 inhibitor to boost other PIs.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Integrase Inhibitors
content: Integrase inhibitors, such as raltegravir and dolutegravir, prevent HIV DNA from integrating into the host cell's genome.

title: Lyme disease – Definition
content: Lyme disease is a multisystemic tick-borne illness caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi (B. afzelii, B. garinii in Europe/Asia). It is transmitted by Ixodes ticks and progresses through early localised, early disseminated, and late disseminated stages.

title: Lyme disease – Epidemiology
content: The incidence of Lyme disease is approximately 12 per 100,000 person-years, with a peak incidence observed in individuals aged 6-15 years.

title: Lyme disease – Aetiology
content: Lyme disease is caused by the Borrelia burgdorferi spirochete. The primary vectors are Ixodes scapularis in the USA and Ixodes ricinus in Europe. The risk of transmission is highest after 36-48 hours of tick attachment.

title: Lyme disease – Early Clinical Features: Erythema Migrans
content: Erythema migrans, a 'bulls-eye' rash, is a hallmark early clinical feature of Lyme disease, appearing 1-4 weeks post-tick bite. It is typically >5cm, painless, slowly enlarges, and is present in approximately 80% of early cases.

title: Lyme disease – Early Clinical Features: Systemic Symptoms
content: Early systemic symptoms of Lyme disease, occurring within 30 days of infection, include headache, lethargy, fever, and arthralgia.

title: Lyme disease – Late Clinical Features: Cardiovascular
content: Late clinical features of Lyme disease, manifesting after 30 days, can include cardiovascular complications such as heart block and peri/myocarditis.

title: Lyme disease – Late Clinical Features: Neurological
content: Neurological manifestations in late Lyme disease (after 30 days) include facial nerve palsy, radicular pain, and meningitis.

title: Lyme disease – Investigations: Clinical Diagnosis
content: Lyme disease is diagnosed clinically if erythema migrans is present, allowing for immediate antibiotic treatment without further testing.

title: Lyme disease – Investigations: Serology
content: ELISA for Borrelia antibodies is the first-line investigation. If negative but Lyme disease is suspected within 4 weeks, repeat ELISA 4-6 weeks later. A positive or equivocal ELISA result warrants a confirmatory immunoblot test.

title: Lyme disease – Management: Early Disease
content: Early Lyme disease is managed with Doxycycline. Amoxicillin is an alternative if Doxycycline is contraindicated, such as during pregnancy.

title: Lyme disease – Management: Disseminated Disease
content: Disseminated Lyme disease requires treatment with Ceftriaxone. Patients should be monitored for a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after the initial antibiotic dose.

title: Lyme disease – Management: Asymptomatic Tick Bites
content: For asymptomatic tick bites, routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended according to NICE guidelines.

title: Lyme disease – Complications: Neuroborreliosis
content: Neuroborreliosis, a complication of Lyme disease, can manifest as lymphocytic meningitis, facial nerve palsy, and radiculoneuritis.

title: Lyme disease – Complications: Lyme Carditis and Chronic Arthritis
content: Lyme carditis, presenting as AV block or myopericarditis, and chronic arthritis are significant complications of Lyme disease.

title: Malaria – Definition
content: Non-falciparum malaria is caused by various Plasmodium species, including P. vivax (the most prevalent), P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi.

title: Malaria – General Clinical Features
content: Common clinical manifestations of non-falciparum malaria include fever, headache, and an enlarged spleen (splenomegaly).

title: Malaria – P. vivax/ovale Fever Pattern
content: Infections with Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale typically present with a cyclical fever occurring approximately every 48 hours.

title: Malaria – P. malariae Fever Pattern
content: Plasmodium malariae infections are characterized by a distinct cyclical fever pattern that recurs every 72 hours.

title: Malaria – P. malariae and Nephrotic Syndrome
content: Plasmodium malariae infection is notably associated with the development of nephrotic syndrome, a kidney disorder.

title: Malaria – P. vivax/ovale Hypnozoite Stage
content: Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale have a hypnozoite liver stage, which can lead to relapses even after initial treatment.

title: Malaria – Management in Chloroquine-Sensitive Areas
content: In regions where malaria is sensitive to chloroquine, treatment options include Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) or chloroquine, as recommended by WHO.

title: Malaria – Management in Chloroquine-Resistant Areas
content: For non-falciparum malaria in areas with chloroquine resistance, Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) is the recommended management.

title: Malaria – Management of P. vivax/ovale Relapse Prevention
content: Following acute treatment for P. vivax or P. ovale malaria, primaquine should be administered to eliminate liver hypnozoites and prevent future relapses. ACTs should be avoided in pregnancy.

title: Meningitis – Definition
content: Meningitis is characterized by inflammation of the meninges, the protective membranes enveloping the brain and spinal cord. The underlying causes of this condition can vary significantly depending on the patient's age group.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (0-3 months)
content: In infants aged 0-3 months, common bacterial causes of meningitis include Group B Streptococcus, which is the most prevalent pathogen in neonates. Other significant causative agents are Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Group B Streptococcus)
content: Group B Streptococcus is a primary bacterial cause of meningitis, particularly noted for its high incidence in neonates (0-3 months). It is considered the most common pathogen responsible for meningitis in this vulnerable age group.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (E. coli)
content: Escherichia coli (E. coli) is a significant bacterial pathogen implicated in meningitis, especially in the youngest patient demographic, specifically infants aged 0-3 months. Its presence necessitates prompt and effective antimicrobial treatment.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Listeria monocytogenes)
content: Listeria monocytogenes is a bacterial cause of meningitis, notably affecting infants aged 0-3 months and individuals over 60 years. It is also a critical pathogen to consider in immunosuppressed patients due to their heightened susceptibility.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (3 months-6 years)
content: For children between 3 months and 6 years, the primary bacterial causes of meningitis include Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae. These pathogens are responsible for the majority of cases in this age bracket.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Neisseria meningitidis)
content: Neisseria meningitidis is a significant bacterial cause of meningitis, particularly prevalent in children aged 3 months to 6 years and adults aged 6-60 years. It is known for its potential to cause outbreaks.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Streptococcus pneumoniae)
content: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading bacterial cause of meningitis across various age groups, including children aged 3 months to 6 years, adults aged 6-60 years, and individuals over 60 years. Vaccination can prevent many cases.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Haemophilus influenzae)
content: Haemophilus influenzae is a bacterial pathogen responsible for meningitis, primarily observed in children aged 3 months to 6 years. The introduction of the Hib vaccine has significantly reduced the incidence of this type of meningitis.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (6-60 years)
content: In individuals aged 6 to 60 years, the most common bacterial pathogens causing meningitis are Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae. These two organisms account for a substantial proportion of meningitis cases in this broad age group.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (>60 years)
content: For patients over 60 years of age, the predominant bacterial causes of meningitis include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Listeria monocytogenes. The elderly population is particularly susceptible to these infections.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Immunosuppressed)
content: Immunosuppressed individuals are at an elevated risk for meningitis caused by specific pathogens. Listeria monocytogenes is a particularly important causative agent to consider in this patient population due to their compromised immune defenses.

title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Group B Streptococcus in Neonates)
content: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is the most frequent bacterial cause of meningitis in neonates, specifically within the 0-3 month age bracket. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial due to the severity of GBS infections in this population.

title: Meningitis – Bacterial CSF Appearance
content: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in bacterial meningitis typically presents with a cloudy or turbid appearance due to the presence of inflammatory cells and bacteria.

title: Meningitis – Bacterial CSF Glucose
content: CSF glucose levels in bacterial meningitis are characteristically low, often less than half of the plasma glucose concentration, reflecting bacterial consumption of glucose.

title: Meningitis – Bacterial CSF Protein
content: Elevated CSF protein levels, typically exceeding 1 g/L, are a common finding in bacterial meningitis, indicating increased vascular permeability and inflammation.

title: Meningitis – Bacterial CSF WBC Count
content: Bacterial meningitis is associated with a high CSF white blood cell (WBC) count, ranging from 10 to 5000 polymorphonuclear leukocytes per cubic millimeter.

title: Meningitis – Viral CSF Appearance
content: CSF in viral meningitis can appear clear or slightly cloudy. The appearance is less turbid than in bacterial infections.

title: Meningitis – Viral CSF Glucose
content: CSF glucose levels in viral meningitis are typically normal, usually 60-80% of plasma glucose. However, some viral causes like mumps or herpes encephalitis can cause low glucose.

title: Meningitis – Viral CSF Protein
content: CSF protein levels in viral meningitis are typically normal or mildly raised, generally less pronounced than in bacterial infections.

title: Meningitis – Viral CSF WBC Count
content: Viral meningitis typically shows a CSF white blood cell (WBC) count between 15 and 1000 lymphocytes per cubic millimeter, with a lymphocytic predominance.

title: Mumps – CSF Glucose in Meningitis
content: Mumps virus can cause meningitis with unusually low CSF glucose levels in a proportion of cases, deviating from the typical normal glucose seen in most viral meningitis.

title: Encephalitis – Herpes CSF Glucose
content: Herpes encephalitis can present with low CSF glucose, a finding that can sometimes overlap with bacterial or tuberculous meningitis, requiring careful differential diagnosis.

title: Meningitis – Tuberculous CSF Appearance
content: CSF in tuberculous meningitis often appears slightly cloudy and may form a fibrin web upon standing, a characteristic finding.

title: Meningitis – Tuberculous CSF Glucose
content: CSF glucose levels in tuberculous meningitis are typically low, often less than half of the plasma glucose, similar to bacterial meningitis.

title: Meningitis – Tuberculous CSF Protein
content: Tuberculous meningitis is characterized by high CSF protein levels, typically exceeding 1 g/L, reflecting significant inflammation and blood-brain barrier disruption.

title: Meningitis – Tuberculous CSF WBC Count
content: CSF white blood cell (WBC) count in tuberculous meningitis ranges from 30 to 300 lymphocytes per cubic millimeter, with a lymphocytic predominance.

title: Tuberculosis – Ziehl-Neelsen Stain Sensitivity
content: The Ziehl-Neelsen stain for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in CSF has a low sensitivity of approximately 20%, making it an unreliable sole diagnostic tool for tuberculous meningitis.

title: Tuberculosis – NAAT for MTB DNA
content: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA are the preferred diagnostic method for tuberculous meningitis due to their higher sensitivity compared to traditional staining.

title: Meningitis – Fungal CSF Appearance
content: CSF in fungal meningitis typically appears cloudy, similar to bacterial meningitis, reflecting the inflammatory response to fungal pathogens.

title: Meningitis – Fungal CSF Glucose
content: CSF glucose levels are low in fungal meningitis, a finding consistent with microbial consumption of glucose, similar to bacterial and tuberculous etiologies.

title: Meningitis – Fungal CSF Protein
content: High CSF protein levels are characteristic of fungal meningitis, indicating an inflammatory response and increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier.

title: Meningitis – Fungal CSF WBC Count
content: Fungal meningitis typically presents with a CSF white blood cell (WBC) count ranging from 20 to 200 lymphocytes per cubic millimeter, primarily lymphocytic.

title: Meningitis – Initial Management: Urgent Transfer
content: Patients with suspected bacterial meningitis require urgent transfer to hospital for immediate medical assessment and intervention.

title: Meningitis – Pre-hospital Benzylpenicillin
content: Administer pre-hospital intramuscular benzylpenicillin if meningococcal disease is suspected, provided it does not delay urgent transfer to hospital.

title: Meningitis – Initial Management: ABC Approach
content: The initial management of suspected bacterial meningitis should always follow the ABC (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) approach to stabilize the patient.

title: Meningitis – Senior Review Warning Signs
content: A senior review is indicated if warning signs are present, such as a rapidly progressive rash, poor perfusion, extreme respiratory or heart rates, abnormal pH/WBC/lactate, GCS <12 or drop of 2, or poor fluid response.

title: Meningitis – Contraindications for Immediate Lumbar Puncture
content: Delay lumbar puncture if severe sepsis/rapidly evolving rash, severe respiratory/cardiac compromise, significant bleeding risk, signs of raised ICP, focal neurological signs, papilloedema, continuous seizures, or GCS ≤9.

title: Meningitis – Lumbar Puncture Procedure
content: If no contraindications for delayed LP, establish IV access, take bloods and blood cultures, then perform lumbar puncture.

title: Meningitis – Antibiotic Administration Timing
content: If lumbar puncture cannot be performed within one hour, administer IV antibiotics immediately after obtaining blood cultures.

title: Meningitis – Antibiotic Regimen (3 months-60 years)
content: For patients aged 3 months to 60 years with suspected bacterial meningitis, the recommended antibiotic is intravenous ceftriaxone.

title: Meningitis – Antibiotic Regimen (≥60 years)
content: Patients aged 60 years and older with suspected bacterial meningitis should receive intravenous ceftriaxone combined with amoxicillin or ampicillin.

title: Meningitis – Antibiotic Regimen (<3 months)
content: For infants younger than 3 months with suspected bacterial meningitis, the antibiotic regimen includes intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin or ampicillin.

title: Meningitis – Vancomycin Indication
content: Intravenous vancomycin should be added to the antibiotic regimen if there is a history of recent prolonged/multiple antibiotic use or travel to areas with resistant pneumococci.

title: Meningitis – Adjunctive Dexamethasone
content: Consider adjunctive IV dexamethasone, especially if pneumococcal meningitis is suspected in adults, ideally before or with the first antibiotic dose, and no later than 12 hours after.

title: Meningitis – Dexamethasone Contraindications
content: Avoid adjunctive dexamethasone in cases of septic shock, meningococcal septicaemia, immunocompromised patients, or post-surgical meningitis.

title: Meningitis – Contact Prophylaxis
content: Oral ciprofloxacin (single dose, preferred) or rifampicin should be offered to close contacts within 7 days before onset. Meningococcal vaccination is given if serotype is known.

title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Definition
content: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a bacterial strain that played a significant role in highlighting the risks associated with infections acquired within healthcare settings.

title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Screening (Elective Admissions)
content: Screening for MRSA is mandatory for all patients scheduled for elective admissions, with exceptions for day patients undergoing termination of pregnancy, ophthalmic surgery, or those admitted to mental health trusts.

title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Screening (Emergency Admissions)
content: Since 2011, all patients admitted as emergencies are required to undergo screening for Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) upon admission to healthcare facilities.

title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Screening Method (Swab Sites)
content: MRSA screening involves collecting samples from the nasal passages and any existing skin lesions or wounds to detect the presence of the bacteria.

title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Screening Method (Swab Technique)
content: For nasal screening, a swab should be carefully rotated around the inner rim of the nose for five seconds. The microbiology form must be clearly marked as 'MRSA screen'.

title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Screening Documentation
content: When submitting samples for MRSA screening, it is crucial to ensure that the microbiology request form is explicitly labeled 'MRSA screen' for proper processing and identification.

title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Carrier Suppression (Nasal)
content: For nasal carriage of MRSA, treatment involves applying mupirocin 2% in white soft paraffin three times daily (TDS) to the nose for a duration of five days.

title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Carrier Suppression (Skin)
content: To suppress MRSA carriage on the skin, chlorhexidine gluconate should be applied once daily (OD) for five days to specific areas including the axilla, groin, and perineum.

title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Infection Treatment (Primary Antibiotics)
content: Effective antibiotics for treating MRSA infections include vancomycin, teicoplanin, and linezolid, which are typically used to combat resistant strains.

title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Infection Treatment (Antibiotics to Avoid Monotherapy)
content: Antibiotics such as rifampicin, macrolides, tetracyclines, and aminoglycosides should not be administered as monotherapy for MRSA infections due to the significant risk of developing resistance.

title: Tuberculosis – Active TB Initial Treatment
content: The initial phase of active tuberculosis treatment, lasting two months, involves a four-drug regimen known as RIPE: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol. This intensive phase aims to rapidly reduce bacterial load and prevent drug resistance.

title: Tuberculosis – Active TB Continuation Treatment
content: Following the initial phase, the continuation phase for active tuberculosis treatment extends for four months. During this period, the regimen typically consists of two drugs: Rifampicin and Isoniazid, to ensure complete eradication of the infection.

title: Tuberculosis – Latent TB 3-Month Regimen
content: Treatment for latent tuberculosis can involve a three-month regimen combining isoniazid and rifampicin, with pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) supplementation to prevent peripheral neuropathy. This option is often preferred for patients under 35 years with hepatotoxicity concerns.

title: Tuberculosis – Latent TB 6-Month Regimen
content: An alternative treatment for latent tuberculosis is a six-month course of isoniazid, also supplemented with pyridoxine. This regimen is typically chosen for HIV or transplant patients due to potential rifamycin interactions, which can complicate other drug therapies.

title: Tuberculosis – Meningeal TB Treatment
content: Meningeal tuberculosis requires a prolonged treatment course of at least 12 months. This regimen includes the addition of corticosteroids to the standard anti-tuberculosis drugs, which helps to reduce inflammation and improve outcomes in this severe form of the disease.

title: Tuberculosis – Directly Observed Therapy (DOT)
content: Directly Observed Therapy (DOT), administered three times a week, is crucial for specific patient groups with tuberculosis. It ensures medication adherence and treatment completion, particularly for homeless individuals with active TB and all prisoners with active or latent TB.

title: Tuberculosis – Rifampicin Adverse Effects
content: Rifampicin, a key anti-TB drug, can cause several adverse effects including potent liver enzyme induction, hepatitis, and flu-like symptoms. Patients may also notice harmless orange discoloration of secretions, such as urine and tears.

title: Tuberculosis – Isoniazid Adverse Effects
content: Isoniazid can lead to peripheral neuropathy, which is preventable with pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) supplementation. Other notable adverse effects include hepatitis, agranulocytosis, and its action as a liver enzyme inhibitor, requiring careful monitoring.

title: Tuberculosis – Pyrazinamide Adverse Effects
content: Pyrazinamide, an anti-TB medication, is associated with adverse effects such as hyperuricaemia, which can precipitate gout. Patients may also experience arthralgia (joint pain), myalgia (muscle pain), and hepatitis, necessitating liver function monitoring.

title: Tuberculosis – Ethambutol Adverse Effects
content: Ethambutol is known for its potential to cause optic neuritis, an inflammation of the optic nerve. Therefore, it is crucial to check visual acuity both before and regularly during treatment to detect and manage this adverse effect promptly.

title: Tuberculosis – Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS)
content: Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) can occur approximately 3-6 weeks after initiating anti-tuberculosis treatment, particularly in immunocompromised patients. It often manifests as paradoxical worsening of existing lesions or the appearance of new ones, such as enlarging lymph nodes.

title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test procedure
content: The Mantoux test involves injecting 0.1ml of Purified Protein Derivative (PPD) intradermally to assess for tuberculosis infection.

title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test reading time
content: Results of the Mantoux test should be interpreted between 48 and 72 hours after the intradermal injection.

title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test negative result
content: An induration of less than 5mm at the injection site typically indicates a negative Mantoux test result.

title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test positive result
content: An induration of 5mm or greater on a Mantoux test suggests tuberculosis infection, irrespective of prior BCG vaccination.

title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test strongly positive result
content: An induration exceeding 15mm in a Mantoux test is considered a strongly positive result, indicating a high likelihood of TB infection.

title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test false negatives
content: False negative Mantoux results can occur in conditions such as miliary tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, HIV, lymphoma, and in infants under 6 months old.

title: Tuberculosis – IGRA indications
content: Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) is utilized when Mantoux test results are positive or inconclusive, or when false negative tuberculin tests are suspected.

title: Tuberculosis – CXR findings in active TB
content: Chest X-ray (CXR) in active tuberculosis may reveal upper lobe cavitation, characteristic of reactivated TB, or bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, though unilateral is more typical of primary TB.

title: Tuberculosis – Sputum smear for diagnosis
content: Diagnosis of tuberculosis often involves sputum smear microscopy, requiring three specimens. It is a rapid and inexpensive method, using Ziehl-Neelsen stain to detect acid-fast bacilli.

title: Tuberculosis – Sputum smear sensitivity
content: Sputum smear for tuberculosis has a sensitivity ranging from 50-80%, which can drop to 20-30% in individuals with HIV infection.

title: Tuberculosis – Sputum culture gold standard
content: Sputum culture is considered the gold standard for tuberculosis diagnosis, offering higher sensitivity than smear or NAAT, and allowing for drug susceptibility testing. Results typically take 1-3 weeks with liquid media.

title: Tuberculosis – NAAT for diagnosis
content: Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) provides rapid tuberculosis diagnosis within 24-48 hours. It is more sensitive than sputum smear but less sensitive than culture.

title: Tuberculosis – All mycobacteria stain positive on Ziehl-Neelsen
content: It is important to note that all mycobacteria will stain positive with the Ziehl-Neelsen stain, not exclusively Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Definition
content: Viral meningitis is characterized by inflammation of the leptomeninges caused by a viral agent. It is generally considered a more benign condition compared to bacterial meningitis, with approximately 3000 confirmed cases reported annually in the UK, though the actual incidence is likely higher.

title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Aetiology
content: The most common causes of viral meningitis are non-polio enteroviruses, including coxsackievirus and echovirus. Other viral agents that can lead to this condition include mumps virus, herpes simplex virus (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), varicella-zoster virus (herpes zoster), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and measles virus.

title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Risk Factors
content: Risk factors for developing viral meningitis include extremes of age, particularly in children under 5 years old and the elderly. Immunocompromised individuals, such as those with renal failure or diabetes, and intravenous drug users (IVDU) are also at increased risk.

title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Clinical Features
content: Common clinical features of viral meningitis include headache, neck stiffness, photophobia (often milder than in bacterial meningitis), confusion, and fever. Less common manifestations, such as focal neurological deficits or seizures, may suggest meningoencephalitis.

title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis CSF Opening Pressure
content: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis in viral meningitis typically reveals an opening pressure ranging from 10 to 20 cmH2O, which is within or slightly above the normal range.

title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis CSF Cell Count
content: CSF findings in viral meningitis usually show a cell count between 10 and 300 cells/µL, predominantly consisting of lymphocytes. This lymphocytic pleocytosis helps differentiate it from bacterial meningitis.

title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis CSF Glucose and Protein
content: CSF analysis for viral meningitis typically shows glucose levels between 2.8-4.2 mmol/L, or approximately two-thirds of the serum glucose level. Protein levels are usually in the range of 0.5-1 g/dL.

title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Diagnosis and Supportive Treatment
content: Diagnosis of viral meningitis is confirmed via lumbar puncture (LP). Management primarily involves supportive treatment. If bacterial meningitis or encephalitis cannot be definitively ruled out, empirical treatment with ceftriaxone and intravenous aciclovir is initiated.

title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Prognosis and Specific Treatment
content: Viral meningitis is generally a self-limiting condition, with symptoms typically resolving within 7-14 days. Aciclovir treatment is specifically indicated if herpes simplex virus (HSV) is suspected as the causative agent.

title: Sepsis – Definition
content: Sepsis is a critical condition characterized by life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from the body's uncontrolled response to an infection. Early recognition and intervention are crucial for improved patient outcomes.

title: Sepsis – Septic Shock Definition
content: Septic shock is a severe form of sepsis, identified by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥65 mmHg and serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. It is associated with significantly higher mortality rates.

title: Sepsis – qSOFA Criteria
content: The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score is a rapid screening tool for sepsis. Criteria include respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation (Glasgow Coma Scale <15), and systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg. A score of ≥2 indicates a high risk of sepsis.

title: Sepsis – Sepsis-6 Bundle
content: The Sepsis-6 bundle outlines key interventions to be initiated within one hour of sepsis recognition. These include obtaining blood cultures, administering intravenous antibiotics, giving an IV fluid bolus (500ml crystalloid), monitoring urine output, measuring serum lactate, and providing high-flow oxygen.

title: Sepsis – Septic Shock Management
content: Management of septic shock primarily involves vasopressor support. Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor to achieve a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥65 mmHg. Hydrocortisone may be considered if the patient remains refractory to vasopressors.

title: Sepsis – Organ Dysfunction Markers
content: Key markers indicating organ dysfunction in sepsis include elevated lactate levels (>2 mmol/L), acute kidney injury (AKI), coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, raised bilirubin, and a reduced Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). These reflect the severity of the host response.

title: Sepsis – Target MAP in Septic Shock
content: In the management of septic shock, the primary hemodynamic goal is to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of ≥65 mmHg. This target ensures adequate organ perfusion while minimizing the risks associated with excessive vasopressor use.

title: Pneumonia – Definition
content: Pneumonia is characterized by an infection affecting the lung parenchyma. It is categorized into community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP), with HAP occurring more than 48 hours post-admission.

title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Streptococcus pneumoniae
content: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most frequent bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), accounting for approximately 80% of cases.

title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Haemophilus influenzae
content: Haemophilus influenzae is another common bacterial pathogen implicated in the development of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP).

title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Staphylococcus aureus
content: Staphylococcus aureus can cause community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), particularly as a secondary infection following an influenza illness.

title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Atypical pathogens
content: Atypical pathogens causing community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) include Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, and Chlamydophila pneumoniae.

title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Klebsiella pneumoniae
content: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a notable cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), frequently observed in individuals with a history of alcoholism.

title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Viruses
content: Various viruses can also be responsible for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) cases.

title: Pneumonia – Clinical features
content: Key clinical features of pneumonia include fever, cough (potentially productive with rusty sputum in pneumococcal cases), pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, tachypnoea, and tachycardia.

title: Pneumonia – Clinical features - Consolidation signs
content: Physical examination may reveal signs of lung consolidation, such as dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing, and increased vocal resonance.

title: Pneumonia – CURB-65 score
content: The CURB-65 score assesses pneumonia severity: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory Rate ≥30/min, Blood Pressure <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic, Age ≥65.

title: Pneumonia – CURB-65 score interpretation
content: CURB-65 score 0-1 suggests home treatment. A score of 2 indicates hospital admission. Scores 3-5 denote severe pneumonia, warranting consideration for ICU care.

title: Pneumonia – Investigations
content: Investigations for pneumonia include a chest X-ray (CXR) showing lobar consolidation, FBC, CRP, U&E, blood cultures, and sputum culture. Urine antigen tests for pneumococcal/Legionella are also used. ABG is performed if severe.

title: Pneumonia – Management (CAP) - CURB-65 0-1
content: For community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) with a CURB-65 score of 0-1, management typically involves oral amoxicillin.

title: Pneumonia – Management (CAP) - CURB-65 2
content: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) with a CURB-65 score of 2 is managed with oral amoxicillin combined with clarithromycin.

title: Pneumonia – Management (CAP) - CURB-65 3-5 (Option 1)
content: Severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) with a CURB-65 score of 3-5 is managed with intravenous (IV) co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin.

title: Pneumonia – Management (CAP) - CURB-65 3-5 (Option 2)
content: Alternatively, severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) with a CURB-65 score of 3-5 can be managed with intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone plus clarithromycin.

title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis A PEP - HNIG Use
content: Hepatitis A post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) with Human Normal Immunoglobulin (HNIG) is reserved for individuals unable to receive the vaccine or requiring rapid protection, such as immunosuppressed patients.

title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis A PEP - Vaccine Preference
content: The Hepatitis A vaccine is the preferred method for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) in most cases, offering effective protection against the virus.

title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis B PEP - Known Responder
content: For Hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) in a known responder (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL) with an HBsAg-positive source, a booster dose of vaccine is indicated.

title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis B PEP - Non-Responder
content: If a non-responder (anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL) is exposed to an HBsAg-positive source, Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and a booster vaccine are given for PEP.

title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis B PEP - Unknown Source
content: For Hepatitis B PEP with an unknown source and a non-responder, both HBIG and a booster vaccine are administered to provide protection.

title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis B PEP - Primary Course
content: A primary course for Hepatitis B PEP involves an accelerated vaccination schedule, potentially with HBIG if the exposure risk is high.

title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis C PEP - No Effective Prophylaxis
content: There is currently no effective post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) available for Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection.

title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis C PEP - Monitoring
content: Following potential Hepatitis C exposure, baseline HCV serology and RNA (PCR) are performed, with repeat HCV RNA at 6 and 12 weeks, and antibody testing at 3 and 6 months.

title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis C PEP - Seroconversion Management
content: If Hepatitis C seroconversion occurs after exposure, early hepatology referral for direct-acting antivirals is crucial for effective treatment.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus – HIV PEP - First-line Regimen
content: First-line HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) typically involves tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine (Truvada) combined with raltegravir.

title: Human immunodeficiency virus – HIV PEP - Timing and Duration
content: HIV PEP should be initiated as soon as possible, ideally within 1-2 hours and no later than 72 hours post-exposure, for a 4-week course.

title: Varicella zoster – VZV PEP - VZIG Use
content: Varicella Zoster Immunoglobulin (VZIG) is recommended for IgG-negative pregnant women or immunosuppressed individuals after significant VZV exposure.

title: Varicella zoster – VZV PEP - Aciclovir Alternative
content: If VZIG is unavailable or more than 10 days have passed since exposure, oral aciclovir can be used for VZV post-exposure prophylaxis.

title: Transmission risks – Needlestick Injuries
content: Needlestick injuries carry varying transmission risks: Hepatitis B 20-30% (if HBeAg positive), Hepatitis C 0.5-2%, and HIV 0.3%.

title: Sepsis – Risk Factors
content: Individuals with hyposplenism are at an elevated risk of developing post-splenectomy sepsis. This severe infection is commonly caused by encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Capnocytophaga canimorsus, often transmitted through dog bites.

title: Sepsis – Vaccination Schedule
content: For patients undergoing splenectomy, essential vaccinations include pneumococcal, Hib, and meningococcal type C. These should ideally be administered two weeks before or after the procedure. The recommended schedule involves MenC + Hib at two weeks post-splenectomy, followed by MenACWY one month later.

title: Sepsis – Ongoing Vaccinations
content: Lifelong vaccination is crucial for individuals post-splenectomy. This includes an annual influenza vaccination to protect against seasonal strains. Additionally, a pneumococcal vaccine booster is required every five years to maintain adequate immunity against Streptococcus pneumoniae.

title: Sepsis – Antibiotic Prophylaxis
content: Patients post-splenectomy typically require antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent severe infections. Penicillin V is commonly prescribed for at least two years, and often until the age of 16. Many patients, particularly those with ongoing risk, may continue lifelong prophylaxis.

title: Sepsis – Diagnosing Hyposplenism
content: The diagnosis of hyposplenism can be suggested by the presence of Howell-Jolly bodies on a blood film, though this method is not entirely reliable. The most sensitive diagnostic technique for assessing splenic function is a radionucleotide-labelled red cell scan.

title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Dysuria
content: Dysuria, characterized by painful or difficult urination, is a common symptom of urinary tract infection (UTI).

title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Frequency
content: Increased urinary frequency, the need to urinate more often than usual, is a typical clinical feature of urinary tract infection (UTI).

title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Urgency
content: Urinary urgency, a sudden and compelling need to pass urine, is a common presentation in patients with urinary tract infection (UTI).

title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Urine appearance
content: Cloudy or offensive-smelling urine can indicate a urinary tract infection (UTI), often due to the presence of bacteria and white blood cells.

title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Lower abdominal pain
content: Lower abdominal pain or discomfort is a frequent symptom reported by individuals experiencing a urinary tract infection (UTI).

title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Low-grade fever
content: A low-grade fever may be present in cases of lower urinary tract infection (UTI), indicating a systemic response to the infection.

title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Acute confusion in elderly
content: In elderly patients, acute confusion or delirium can be the primary or sole presentation of a urinary tract infection (UTI).

title: Urinary tract infection – Investigations: Urine dipstick findings
content: A urine dipstick showing positive nitrite or the presence of leukocytes and red blood cells strongly suggests a urinary tract infection (UTI).

title: Urinary tract infection – Investigations: Urine culture indications
content: Urine culture is indicated for UTI diagnosis in women over 65, those with recurrent UTIs, pregnant women, men, patients with haematuria, and catheterized individuals.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (non-pregnant women): First-line antibiotics
content: For non-pregnant women with UTI, NICE guidelines recommend trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin for 3 days as first-line antibiotic treatment.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (non-pregnant women): Urine culture
content: In non-pregnant women with UTI, a urine culture should be sent if the patient is over 65 years old or presents with haematuria.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (pregnant women): Antibiotic choices
content: Pregnant women with UTI can be treated with nitrofurantoin (avoid near term), amoxicillin, or cefalexin for 7 days.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (pregnant women): Trimethoprim contraindication
content: Trimethoprim is teratogenic in the first trimester and should be avoided throughout pregnancy due to potential harm to the fetus.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (pregnant women): Asymptomatic bacteriuria
content: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnant women must be treated to prevent complications such as pyelonephritis, which poses risks to both mother and fetus.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (pregnant women): Test of cure
content: A test of cure is essential after treating UTI in pregnant women to confirm eradication of the infection and prevent recurrence.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (men): Antibiotic regimen
content: For men with UTI, a 7-day course of trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin is typically prescribed.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (men): Pre-antibiotic urine culture
content: In men, a urine culture should be obtained before initiating antibiotic treatment for UTI to guide appropriate therapy.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (men): Urology referral
content: Urology referral is not routinely necessary for a single, uncomplicated urinary tract infection in men.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (catheterised): Asymptomatic bacteriuria
content: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterized patients should not be treated with antibiotics, as it is often colonization rather than infection.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (catheterised): Symptomatic treatment
content: Symptomatic urinary tract infection in catheterized patients requires a 7-day course of antibiotics.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management (catheterised): Catheter removal/change
content: Consider removing or changing the catheter if it has been in place for more than 7 days in a symptomatic catheterized UTI patient.

title: Acute pyelonephritis – Management: Hospital admission
content: Hospital admission should be considered for patients diagnosed with acute pyelonephritis, especially if severe or complicated.

title: Acute pyelonephritis – Management: Antibiotic regimen
content: Acute pyelonephritis in non-pregnant individuals is typically managed with a broad-spectrum cephalosporin or quinolone for 10-14 days.

title: Vaccinations – Live Attenuated Vaccine Types
content: Live attenuated vaccines utilize weakened forms of the pathogen to induce immunity. They are generally not recommended for immunocompromised individuals.

title: Vaccinations – Examples of Live Attenuated Vaccines
content: Examples of live attenuated vaccines include BCG, MMR, intranasal influenza, oral rotavirus, oral polio, yellow fever, and oral typhoid.

title: Vaccinations – Live Attenuated Vaccine Contraindication
content: Live attenuated vaccines are generally contraindicated in individuals who are immunocompromised due to the risk of uncontrolled infection.

title: Vaccinations – Inactivated Vaccine Types
content: Inactivated vaccines contain killed versions of the pathogen, which cannot replicate but still trigger an immune response.

title: Vaccinations – Examples of Inactivated Vaccines
content: Examples of inactivated vaccines include rabies, hepatitis A, and intramuscular influenza vaccines.

title: Vaccinations – Toxoid Vaccine Types
content: Toxoid vaccines use inactivated bacterial toxins to stimulate an immune response against the toxin, rather than the bacteria itself.

title: Vaccinations – Examples of Toxoid Vaccines
content: Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccines are examples of toxoid vaccines.

title: Vaccinations – Subunit/Conjugate Vaccine Types
content: Subunit vaccines contain only specific parts of the pathogen (e.g., proteins, sugars), while conjugate vaccines link these parts to a carrier protein to enhance immune response.

title: Vaccinations – Examples of Subunit/Conjugate Vaccines
content: Examples include pneumococcal (conjugate), Haemophilus (conjugate), meningococcal (conjugate), hepatitis B, and HPV vaccines.

title: Vaccinations – mRNA Vaccine Types
content: mRNA vaccines deliver genetic instructions to cells to produce a viral protein, triggering an immune response.

title: Vaccinations – Examples of mRNA Vaccines
content: Some COVID-19 vaccines are examples of mRNA vaccine technology.

title: Vaccinations – Viral Vector Vaccine Types
content: Viral vector vaccines use a modified virus to deliver genetic material that prompts an immune response against the target pathogen.

title: Vaccinations – Examples of Viral Vector Vaccines
content: Some Ebola and COVID-19 vaccines are examples of viral vector vaccine technology.

title: Influenza – Vaccine Indications: Age and Chronic Respiratory Disease
content: Influenza vaccination is indicated for individuals over 65 years old and those with chronic respiratory diseases, including asthmatics on inhaled steroids.

title: Influenza – Vaccine Indications: Chronic Cardiac and Renal Disease
content: Indications for influenza vaccine include chronic heart disease and chronic kidney disease stages 3-5.

title: Influenza – Vaccine Indications: Chronic Liver, Neurological Disease, and Diabetes
content: Influenza vaccination is recommended for individuals with chronic liver disease, chronic neurological disease, and diabetes mellitus.

title: Influenza – Vaccine Indications: Immunosuppression and Asplenia
content: Immunosuppression and asplenia are key indications for influenza vaccination.

title: Influenza – Vaccine Indications: Pregnancy, Healthcare Workers, and Care Home Residents
